The alarm hasn’t rung yet, but the room already knows it’s morning. Light slips through the blinds in thin, golden slices, catching dust motes that drift like slow stars. There’s a quiet hum here—the refrigerator cycling on, a distant car door closing three streets over, the breath of someone sleeping down the hall. These are the sounds no one writes poetry about, yet they’re the architecture of daily life. I sit on the edge of the bed, feet touching cool wood, and let the silence settle before it breaks into routine.

Coffee first. Always coffee. The grind of beans is a kind of meditation, rhythmic and predictable. Water boils. The pour creates a dark bloom. Steam rises in curling ribbons that vanish before they reach the ceiling. I carry the mug to the window. Outside, the neighborhood wakes in fragments: a dog barking twice, then stopping; a neighbor pulling curtains back with sharp, practiced motions; the faint screech of a bicycle chain shifting gears. Nothing grand. Everything necessary.

I used to think meaning lived only in crescendos—in departures, arrivals, confessions, breakups, promotions, funerals. But lately, I’ve noticed how most of us are just tending fires. Not blazing them. Tending them. Adding a log here, coaxing embers there, watching them shrink and swell with the wind. Life isn’t a single arc. It’s a thousand small adjustments made in half-darkness, guided by instinct and habit and the vague hope that warmth will outlast the cold.

On the desk lies a notebook I haven’t opened in months. Its pages are blank except for a pressed leaf from October, brittle now, veined like tiny rivers. I remember picking it up because it had the exact shade of copper I’d been trying to describe in a poem I never finished. Poetry, I’ve learned, often ends where language does—right before understanding begins. We draft anyway. We send emails we edit into oblivion. We love people knowing full well we’ll disappoint them, and ourselves, along the way. Still, we show up. That’s the miracle. Not perfection. Persistence.

Rain will come later. It always does when you’re certain skies will clear. The forecast said sunshine, but forecasts are guesses dressed in authority. I trust the smell instead—the metallic tang in the air, the way clouds gather heavier than they should, the sudden stillness of birds. Weather doesn’t negotiate. It simply arrives. We prepare or we don’t. Either way, we get wet or we dry.

I think about my grandmother’s kitchen. Not the photographs, but the texture of it: chipped enamel sinks, jars of dried herbs hanging from wooden beams, the particular weight of a cast-iron skillet warmed too long on the stove. She didn’t speak much about her life. She cooked through it. Measured flour by sight, stirred soup until her arms ached, wiped counters with a towel that smelled of lemon and woodsmoke. She understood something I’m still learning: care isn’t dramatic. It’s repetition. It’s showing up to chop onions, fold laundry, water plants, answer texts from people who haven’t replied in years. Love lives in the maintenance.

Sometimes I walk without destination. No podcast, no playlist, just footsteps on pavement that remembers every footfall before mine. Potholes fill with rainwater, reflecting fractured sky. Sidewalk cracks host dandelions defying zoning laws. A child drops an ice cream cone; the adult beside him sighs, then kneels, then shares what’s left on the ground for a startled pigeon. Small collisions. Temporary grace. I collect these without meaning to. They accumulate like pebbles in a pocket—light until you realize your jeans weigh more than they should.

There’s a difference between waiting and anticipating. Waiting is passive, heavy, filled with hollow hours. Anticipating leans forward. It hums. It trusts that something is coming, even if you can’t name it. I’ve spent years mistaking the two. Now I try to tell them apart by their posture. One slumps. The other stands straight, eyes scanning the horizon.

Evening approaches like a slow exhale. Shadows stretch longer. Streetlights flicker on one by one, hesitating, then committing. I make tea instead of coffee this time. Chamomile. It tastes like warm grass and quiet consent. I don’t know why I chose it. Maybe because I needed permission to rest. Permission I rarely grant myself.

Memory is unreliable. Not broken, just selective. It keeps the moments that comfort and discards the ones that ache. That’s its purpose, I suppose. Survival. But sometimes I wish I could access the lost files—the exact tone of a voice at midnight, the smell of a coat worn ten years ago, the feeling of standing on a train platform before a journey that changed everything. Those things are gone. Or maybe they’re just hiding behind ordinary days, waiting for a familiar scent, a song, a certain angle of light to slip through.

I write this not because it’s profound, but because it’s true. Truth doesn’t need polish. It needs witness. You’re reading it now. That’s enough.

The night deepens. Crickets begin their nightly report. Somewhere, a clock ticks, marking time that passes whether we notice or not. I close my eyes. Let the house settle. Let my shoulders drop. Tomorrow will bring new routines, new small fractures, new chances to tend the fire. Until then, I rest. Not out of surrender, but recognition. Rest isn’t defeat. It’s calibration.

I watch the moon rise—not dramatically, but steadily, like something that has done this for millennia and has no reason to hurry. It paints the floorboards silver. Dust settles. The world turns. I breathe. In. Out. The same rhythm my heart has kept since before I knew what breathing meant. 

That’s all. Just this. Living. Observing. Existing in the space between intention and accident. It’s messy. It’s finite. It’s entirely mine. And somehow, impossibly, it’s beautiful.
